cards.title: Hiring Generalists First, Spikes Later
cards.summary: Match ecommerce team hiring to stage: adaptable generalists during 0-to-1, world-class specialists ("spikes") once the operation scales.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to hire another generalist ops/marketing person or a narrowly specialized operator (supply chain, demand planning, paid media) as your store grows.
steps: Identify your stage. In the 0-to-1 phase, favor generalists who can cover many tasks with high adaptability — e.g. one person running product listings, email, and basic ad management. As the business scales into a growth phase, that coverage model starts to break down.

Define the "spike" you actually need: a world-class specialist in one or two discrete areas such as supply chain, demand planning or paid media. The source's framework is that scale rewards depth in specific functions, not continued breadth.

Audit where your current team is over-extended before posting a role. Map the tasks that are consuming the most hours against the tasks that most affect revenue (e.g. demand forecasting error causing stockouts vs. listing upkeep) and hire a spike against the higher-leverage gap.
When upgrading a seat, expect to move from one generalist doing everything to a small number of specialized owners with clearer handoffs; plan the process documentation that handoff requires.
caveats: The generalist-to-spike transition is a stage heuristic, not a fixed headcount rule; small stores with narrow catalogs may stay generalist longer.
A spike can underperform in a lean environment where they have no support team — see the risk-identification card before hiring one.

cards.title: Screen Out Candidates Who Need Large Support Teams
cards.summary: Resume experience alone misleads — check whether a candidate has operated with execution autonomy or has always relied on big support teams.
cards.use_when: Interviewing for an ecommerce ops, supply chain or paid media role where the hire must run lean without a supporting department.
steps: Treat a strong resume as necessary but not sufficient. The source warns against hiring purely on past resume experience when the candidate came from a large organization with heavy support.

Probe for autonomy: ask what they personally owned end-to-end, what they built without a team, and where they had to make calls without escalation. Candidates used to big support teams may stall when dropped into a lean store environment.

Translate the role's reality into the interview: describe your actual constraints (no analyst, no agency, limited budget) and ask the candidate to describe a comparable constraint they operated in. Their answer reveals whether they can execute at that level.

Use the source's specific filter — ask what the candidate would regret or cite if they left the company in three months. The stated purpose is to surface true motivations and alignment with growth pressure, not to trick them.
caveats: This interview filter is a source-recommended technique for evaluating motivation and fit under growth pressure, not a validated predictive test.
Do not read big-company experience as disqualifying on its own; the question is whether the candidate has genuine execution autonomy.

cards.title: Run a High-Velocity Operational Pace Deliberately
cards.summary: Treat speed and velocity as an existential competitive advantage, and avoid comfort traps by continuously tightening execution timelines.
cards.use_when: Setting execution cadence for ecommerce launches, catalog refreshes, campaign tests or site improvements when the team has slipped into a comfortable rhythm.
steps: Adopt the source's stance that speed and velocity are an existential competitive advantage for a scaling ecommerce business — not merely a preference. Frame timelines accordingly when planning a launch, a PDP overhaul or a new acquisition test.
Watch for comfort traps: routines where the team is busy but timelines keep stretching. The source's remedy is to raise the bar on execution timelines rather than accept the drift.
Apply the pace at the level of concrete ecommerce milestones — e.g. set explicit ship dates for a landing page test, a replenishment campaign or a new bundle, and hold the date rather than the scope.

Pair high intensity with the hiring logic above: a pace that expects autonomy and speed only works if the people in the seats can execute lean. Don't set velocity targets the team structurally cannot meet.
caveats: "Speed as existential" is the source's management philosophy, not a measured law; high-intensity pace can backfire if applied without adequate staffing or process.

input.text:
21-OPS / team and business operations

Goes here. Structuring the ecommerce business, organizational design, hiring, process automation, project management, 3PL negotiations, supply chain visibility, forecasting, internal creativity management, and leadership frameworks.

Not here.

Paid advertising strategy, budgeting, or customer acquisition -> 11-ADC

Brand naming, visual identity, and positioning -> 10-MCR

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details management and leadership frameworks for scaling an ecommerce team, contrasting generalists versus specialized "spikes," setting high-intensity operational paces, and evaluating talent using precise interview filters. modules: [OPS] topics: [organizational design, hiring] tier: 3 scope_hint: baseline

Topics. organizational design / Scaling team structures from early stage to growth phase. Moving from hiring generalists (who handle multiple tasks with high adaptability during the 0-to-1 phase) to hiring "spikes" (world-class specialists in discrete operational areas like supply chain, demand planning, or paid media) as the company scales. Setting high-intensity operational paces ("speed and velocity") and avoiding comfort traps by raising the bar on execution timelines. hiring / Evaluating candidates through direct questioning and risk identification. Avoiding hiring based purely on past resume experience if the candidate is accustomed to large support teams rather than working lean. Utilizing specific interview filters, such as asking what a candidate would regret or cite if they chose to leave the company in three months, to evaluate their true motivations and alignment with growth pressure.

Look for. The definition of a "spike": a world-class specialist in one or two specific areas, contrasted with early-stage generalists who handle multiple tasks. The strategic approach to hiring: evaluating whether candidates are used to execution autonomy or reliant on large teams. The management philosophy on pace: driving speed and velocity as an existential competitive advantage.

Skip. Discussions about $2 luxury pricing, RTD beverage formulation, sodium milligrams, manufacturing moqs, or retail distribution broker strategies, as those belong in 10-MCR (Creative & Brand) or 21-OPS supply chain sub-topics.

Scope mix. Baseline mixed with edge (founder management style).

Volume. 10 to 15.
